design_detail: Cross-sectional web survey (REDCap) of Kentucky's 120 elected county coroners (deputy coroners excluded), 5 April to 31 May 2016, delivered in four stages by a modified Dillman approach: an e-mail with the link, a reminder ten days later, completion at the Kentucky Coroners Association annual conference with study staff present, and a last-chance e-mail; e-mail addresses were found for 105 of the 120. Questions covered whether drug overdose investigations had changed since the 2012 toxicology-testing law (expanded in 2015 to require testing of all decedents in coroner investigations) and how, factors in requesting an autopsy, barriers and facilitators to coroner-collected toxicology samples, uses of toxicology results, and barriers to listing specific drugs on death certificates. The questions were reviewed by a focus group (the chief medical examiner, the medical examiner office's coroner liaison, the president of the coroners' association and two elected coroners). Responses were compared across strata (years of service, concurrent position, two kinds of training, jurisdiction size, office budget, assigned regional medical examiner office) with chi-square and Fisher exact tests. No death records, testing volumes or death certificates were analysed.
can_establish: What 48 of Kentucky's 120 elected coroners reported in spring 2016 about changes in their drug overdose investigations since the toxicology-testing mandate, how they used toxicology results, and what they saw as barriers and facilitators to testing and to naming specific drugs on death certificates, with how these reports differed by experience, training, jurisdiction size, budget and region.
cannot_establish: Whether the mandate changed how many deaths were tested, autopsied or certified with specific drugs (no records were examined and there is no measurement before the mandate), how many drug overdose deaths or drugs involved were missed or wrongly certified in either direction, or what the 72 coroners who did not respond would have said; self-reports about complying with a state law may be inflated, as the authors note.

sample.recruitment: A census of all 120 elected county coroners in Kentucky; deputy coroners excluded. E-mail addresses came from the Kentucky Coroners Association and county or government websites (105 found); the third stage was completion in person at the association's annual conference, where updated e-mails were also requested (Methods › Study Population; Methods › Survey Design and Administration, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Elected coroners only. Eligibility for the office is age 24, one year's residence in the county and two in the state; no training in medicine or forensic pathology is required (Methods › Study Population).
sample.demographics: Table 1: 37 (77.1%) served jurisdictions under 50,000 people and 36 (76.6%) had office budgets under $50,000; 47 (98%) held another position (funeral director 28, 58.3%; healthcare professional 12, 25.0%; other 7, 14.6%; the text adds law enforcement, 13%, which Table 1 does not show); 39 (83.0%) reported specific training in drug overdose death investigation and 41 (87.2%) in collecting samples and using toxicology results. Years of service: the all-respondents column gives 20 (42.5%) under ten years and 27 (57.5%) ten or more, but the same rows' phase columns and Tables 2 to 4 give 27 and 20 (see reporting issues). Regions: Eastern 22 (45.8%), Chief medical examiner region 14 (29.2%), Western 8 (16.7%), Northern 4 (8.3%).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one-time survey). Item non-response: one respondent missing for years of service, for each kind of training and for budget; several Table 3 items have 46 or 47 answers.
sample.selection_effects: Response 40% (48/120; 95% CI 32% to 49%, editors' Wilson interval), covering 30.8% (Northern), 33.3% (Western), 43.1% (Eastern) and 43.8% (Chief medical examiner region) of each region's counties. Non-response was checked only by comparing respondents across the four stages on demographic items, with no significant differences reported (Methods › Survey Design and Administration, 3rd paragraph), not against non-respondents. Some answers were given at the coroners' conference with study staff present. The authors note selection bias, and that respondents may have presented themselves as complying with the law (Limitations, 2nd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: The 'exposure' is the state mandate: a 2012 law requiring postmortem toxicology testing where the cause of death is unknown, expanded in 2015 to all decedents for whom a coroner investigation is required, with enhanced coroner training (Introduction, 5th paragraph). It applied to every respondent; its effect was measured only by the respondent's yes/no answer to whether drug overdose investigations had changed since 2012 and which kinds of change had occurred. Strata: years of service (ten-year threshold), concurrent position, self-reported training, jurisdiction size (50,000 people), office budget ($50,000), assigned regional medical examiner office.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable: no deaths or drugs were analysed. The survey asked about barriers to listing all drugs involved, including lack of room on the electronic death certificate.

comparison.controls: No unexposed group and no measurement before the mandate. Comparisons are between strata of respondents (for example under ten years of service against ten or more; the Eastern region against all other regions).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Caseloads, staffing and actual testing and autopsy volumes before and after the mandate were not measured. Strata overlap (small jurisdictions have small budgets; the Eastern region holds most of Kentucky's Appalachian counties, many of them economically disadvantaged) and were compared one at a time without adjustment.

outcomes.instruments: Investigator-designed online questionnaire (REDCap) reviewed for terminology, sensitivity and procedures by the five-member focus group; no other validation or piloting is reported. Items: whether investigations had changed since the 2012 law and how (more investigations, higher caseload, more toxicology, more autopsies); how often factors affect autopsy requests; barriers and facilitators to coroner-collected toxicology samples; what is relied on to determine the cause of a suspected overdose death; how often toxicology results are used to complete death certificates and to inform state agencies; barriers to listing specific drugs.
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation reported. Self-report about compliance with a legal mandate invites socially desirable answers (authors' limitation).
outcomes.operationalization: Impact of the mandate = the share of respondents reporting that investigations had changed and in what way; 'uptake' is inferred from these self-reports. No deaths were counted and nobody's certification was checked.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 18 tabulated items were each compared across 3 to 7 strata: 82 tabulated tests (editors' count of Tables 2 to 4), plus untabulated comparisons in the text. 16 tabulated tests have p<0.05, and four further cells with p between 0.0518 and 0.0580 are flagged as significant at 0.05.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages with chi-square or Fisher exact p-values; no confidence intervals, effect sizes or adjusted analyses. Editors' Wilson 95% intervals: investigations changed 28/48, 58% (44% to 71%); always use toxicology results to complete the death certificate 30/48, 63% (48% to 75%). Recomputed from the printed counts (editors' calculation), most printed p-values match uncorrected chi-square tests and some match Fisher's exact test; where they match chi-square, Fisher's test gives larger values: information gained by experience printed 0.0366, Fisher 0.064; time to collect samples by concurrent position printed 0.0497, Fisher 0.062; lack of facilities by experience printed 0.0404 (which matches the likelihood-ratio chi-square), Fisher 0.059; limited finances by experience printed 0.0564, Fisher 0.105; using toxicology results for the certificate by experience printed 0.0264, Fisher 0.036.
analysis.covariates: None: each comparison is a single stratification.
analysis.selective_reporting: Several results are given only in the text as 'data not shown' or without a table (what coroners rely on, decedent factors in autopsy decisions, training and medical-examiner help as facilitators, the condition of the body and knowing when to collect as barriers, all barriers to listing drugs), without denominators or tests. Table 4 prints identical values in every cell for 'presence of drug paraphernalia at scene' and 'toxicology results'.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 48 respondents, with strata as small as 6 (no toxicology training), 8 (no drug overdose training) and 11 (large jurisdiction; large budget); most stratified comparisons could not detect moderate differences, and the non-significant ones do not show that groups were alike.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 48 responding coroners (40% of 120), 58% said drug overdose investigations had changed since the 2012 law; 58% reported more toxicology testing, 48% more investigations, 40% a higher caseload and 35% more autopsies, and over 26% all four. 63% said they always use toxicology results to complete death certificates and 42% always use them to inform state agencies. 83% named lack of room on the certificate as a barrier to listing specific drugs, 73% the time in hospital between overdose and death, 54% delays in toxicology results and 47% the absence of a requirement to list drugs. No death records were examined.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and first objective present the study as measuring the impact of the mandate, but impact was measured only through coroners' own reports. The Discussion opens by saying that approximately one-half of coroners reported increases in both toxicology testing and autopsy requests; Table 2 gives 58% for toxicology and 35% for autopsies, and the share reporting both is not given. The Conclusion states that the legislation "has had significant impacts" and that most Kentucky coroners reported more testing through increased autopsy referrals, which generalizes from 48 respondents to all coroners and is contradicted by the 35% who reported more autopsies. Experience differences in valuing testing rest partly on the choice of test (the information-gained difference is significant by uncorrected chi-square but not by Fisher's exact test), and an Eastern-region difference of 32% against 28% is called statistically significant. The Discussion says experience 'affected the uptake of toxicology testing requests' (2nd paragraph) and location 'impacted the uptake' (6th paragraph), yet reports of more toxicology testing did not differ by years of service (55.6% against 60%, p = 0.76) or by region (59.1% against 57.7%, p = 0.92; Table 2): these statements rest on attitude and barrier items. It says toxicology training addresses the barrier of restricted space on the electronic certificate (4th paragraph), whereas trained coroners reported lack of room more often (88% against 50%; Results, 9th paragraph). Its statement that the epidemic has more than quadrupled coroner caseloads (5th paragraph) has no data or citation; the survey asked only whether caseloads had risen (39.6% said yes). The policy implication (without uptake, overdose deaths and the drugs involved may be undercounted) and the statement that trained coroners list fewer non-relevant drugs are arguments, not findings of this survey. The abstract's own conclusion, that uptake is not yet complete, is cautiously worded, but it rests on the share of coroners reporting increases (Discussion, 1st paragraph); coroners who already tested before the mandate would also report no increase, and no item asked whether all decedents are now tested.

timeline.event: Kentucky law requires coroners and medical examiners to conduct postmortem toxicology testing where the cause of death is unknown (KRS 72.026, as described in the Introduction).

Warner et al.: about 25% of US drug-poisoning death certificates in 2010 named no specific drug, and centralized medical-examiner states named drugs more often than decentralized coroner states (as summarized in this paper's Introduction, reference 5).

National Association of Medical Examiners position paper on opioid deaths, recommending autopsy of all drug-poisoning deaths and listing every responsible substance (reference 10, the republished 2013 recommendations).
Kentucky mandate expanded to toxicology testing of all decedents in coroner investigations, with enhanced coroner training.
This survey of Kentucky's elected coroners (April and May).
Buchanich et al., cited in the Introduction as early indication that state efforts improved the accuracy of Kentucky's drug-poisoning death certificates (reference 2).
Updated National Association of Medical Examiners position paper on deaths related to opioids and other drugs (not cited by this paper; on the same reading list).

replication.where_it_stands: No repeat of the survey and no record-based evaluation of the mandate is cited. The paper documents how Kentucky's elected coroners, most of them without medical training and most holding other jobs, described their practice and its obstacles a year after the 2015 expansion. Whether the mandate changed testing or the naming of drugs on certificates must be taken from studies of the records themselves, not from this survey.

funding.funder: Cooperative Agreement Number 5 NU17CE002732-04-00, funded by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; the contents are the authors' responsibility and do not necessarily represent the official views of the CDC or the Department of Health and Human Services.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors, reviewers, editors and publication staff do not report any relevant conflicts of interest; the authors have no other financial relationships relevant to the manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors are at the University of Kentucky, Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center; Bunn and Slavova are named as principal investigators of the study. The Introduction cites the same group's description of Kentucky's drug overdose fatality surveillance system (reference 12, Hargrove et al., 2018), so the authors evaluate practices that feed their own centre's surveillance. Received 10 December 2018, accepted 31 January 2019; the survey was run in 2016.

what_would_settle_it: A record-based study in Kentucky of the share of drug overdose deaths with toxicology testing, with autopsy and with specific drugs named on the certificate before 2012, from 2012 to 2015 and after 2015, by county and coroner characteristics and against a state without a mandate, together with a re-review of a sample of certificates against the toxicology reports to count drugs missed and drugs listed that played no part.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to address the target population
domains.note: All 120 elected coroners, the officials who certify coroner cases; deputy coroners, who also investigate, were excluded by design.

domains.domain: 2. Study participants sampled in an appropriate way
domains.note: A census rather than a sample, but e-mail contact existed for 105 of 120, and one stage was completed at the coroners' conference with study staff present.
48 respondents: headline percentages carry 95% intervals of about plus or minus 14 points (editors' calculation), and strata of 6 to 11 respondents carry most comparisons.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Kentucky's hybrid system, coroners' statutory duties and eligibility, and Table 1's characteristics are described; the years-of-service figures conflict between Table 1 and Tables 2 to 4.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis conducted with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Coverage of each region's counties is shown (31% to 44%), but non-respondents are not otherwise described.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods used for identification of the condition
domains.note: An unvalidated questionnaire asking officials to report their own compliance with a state law; no records were used to check any answer.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online questionnaire for all, but some respondents completed it at the conference with study staff present.

No confidence intervals; about 82 uncorrected tests; the test (uncorrected chi-square, likelihood-ratio chi-square or Fisher's exact test) varies from row to row, and several differences called significant are significant only by chi-square; p-values above 0.05 flagged as significant; at least two printed p-values cannot be produced from their counts.

domains.domain: 9. Response rate adequate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: 40% response, assessed only by comparing early and late respondents; the authors acknowledge selection and social-desirability bias.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence, because the paper is a one-time survey of how common certain practices and views are among Kentucky's elected coroners; it measures no deaths and no testing. Editors' summary: high risk of bias, from a 40% response, self-report on compliance with a law, a small sample and an error-prone statistical analysis. Citable for: what responding coroners reported in 2016, with the response rate and the self-report stated (58% said investigations had changed since the 2012 mandate; 58% reported more toxicology testing and 35% more autopsies; 63% always use toxicology results to complete the death certificate; 83% named lack of room on the certificate as a barrier to listing every drug); and for the setting it describes (elected coroners without required medical training, most with other jobs, certifying drug deaths with or without autopsy, with state-funded toxicology). Not citable for: the mandate's effect on testing, autopsy or certification; any number of drug deaths or drugs missed or wrongly attributed; or the weaker subgroup differences. The strongest subgroup results are higher caseloads in larger jurisdictions (82% against 27%, p=0.0033) and less discomfort with sample collection among coroners who are funeral directors (4% against 40%, p=0.0026).

key_findings.finding: Who decides in this setting: Kentucky has a hybrid system in which elected county coroners investigate and certify the cause and manner of death for coroner cases, including drug-poisoning deaths, within ten days, with or without referral for autopsy to one of four regional medical examiner offices; the State Medical Examiner's Office funds all toxicology testing, collection kits and shipping. When a medical examiner does the autopsy, the toxicology report is interpreted in the autopsy report with a suggested cause and manner; when the coroner collects the samples, the coroner interprets the results. No training in medicine or forensic pathology is required for election; newly elected coroners must complete 40 hours of basic death-investigation training.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph; Methods › Study Population; Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph and Table 1 (the four regions)
key_findings.note: The four regional offices are named in Results, 1st paragraph and Table 1, not in the Introduction. The Introduction cites reference 9 (Manini et al. 2011, on agreement between medical examiners and medical toxicologists about cause of death) for the State Medical Examiner's Office funding all toxicology, which looks like a miscitation.

key_findings.finding: The mandate: a 2012 Kentucky law required coroners and medical examiners to conduct postmortem toxicology testing where the cause of death is unknown; in 2015 it was expanded to all decedents for whom a coroner investigation is required, supported by enhanced coroner training on drug-poisoning death investigation and certification.

48 of 120 elected coroners responded (40%); e-mail addresses had been found for 105. Respondents covered 43.8% of counties in the Chief medical examiner region, 43.1% in the Eastern, 33.3% in the Western and 30.8% in the Northern region. 77% served jurisdictions under 50,000 people and 77% had budgets under $50,000; 98% held another position, 58% as funeral directors; 83% reported training in drug overdose death investigation and 87% in toxicology sampling and use.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Survey Design and Administration, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 28 of 48 respondents (58.3%) said drug overdose investigations had changed since the 2012 law; 28 (58.3%) reported more toxicology testing requested, 23 (47.9%) more investigations, 19 (39.6%) a higher caseload and 17 (35.4%) more autopsies; over 26% reported all four (not tabulated). Whether investigations had changed did not differ significantly by experience, training, jurisdiction, budget or region (text), nor by concurrent position (Table 2 only, p = 0.84).

A higher caseload was reported by 10 of 37 coroners (27%) in jurisdictions under 50,000 people against 9 of 11 (82%) in larger ones (p=0.0033), and by 10 of 36 (28%) with budgets under $50,000 against 8 of 11 (73%) with larger budgets (p=0.0073).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, jurisdiction size and office budget

key_findings.finding: 30 of 48 (62.5%) always use toxicology results to complete the death certificate (16 of 20, 80%, with ten or more years of service against 13 of 27, 48%, with fewer; p=0.0264), and 20 (41.7%) always use them to inform state agencies (Eastern region 5 of 22, 23%, against 15 of 26, 58%, elsewhere; p=0.0144). 38% always rely on toxicology results to determine the cause of a suspected overdose death (18 of 48 in Table 4, in a row that duplicates the paraphernalia row, although the text says the data are not shown); 25% always rely on autopsy findings (not tabulated). Table 4 also gives the medical history as always relied on by 26 of 48 (54.2%), an item the text does not mention.
key_findings.note: The experience comparison is significant by uncorrected chi-square; Fisher's exact test gives p=0.036 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Decisions to request an autopsy: decedent factors that always affected the decision were an unknown suspected cause (58%), the decedent's age (19%) and a suspected overdose (15%) (not tabulated); system factors that affected the decision (how often is not stated) were the availability of toxicology results without an autopsy report (76%), limited financial resources (31%) and distance to the regional office (29%); the text cites Table 3, which holds only the finances item, recorded as a factor at some point (15 of 48, 31.2%). Limited finances were cited by 11 of 22 Eastern-region coroners (50%) against 4 of 26 (15%) elsewhere (p=0.0099).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3, not enough financial resources
key_findings.note: The text also contrasts coroners with under ten years of service (41%) and more (15%); that p-value is 0.0564, flagged as significant at 0.05, and Fisher's exact test gives 0.105 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Barriers to coroner-collected toxicology samples: condition of the body (53%), convenience of autopsy (49%), knowing when to collect (40%), lack of facilities (30%), lack of staffing (24%), time to collect (19% in the text, 14 of 47, 30%, in Table 3) and discomfort with collection (19%). Facilitators judged always helpful: state-subsidized kits (67%), information gained (64%), medical examiners' help with interpretation (62%), training (59%); the last two are given in the text only (Table 3 holds information gained and kits). Coroners who were funeral directors were less often uncomfortable with collection (1 of 27, 4%, against 8 of 20, 40%; p=0.0026).

Barriers to listing the specific drugs on death certificates: not enough room to list them all (83%), time in hospital between overdose and death (73%), delay in toxicology results (54%) and no requirement to list drugs (47%); Eastern-region coroners cited lack of room more often (95% against 73%) and the lack of a requirement more often (75% against 24%), and coroners with toxicology training cited lack of room more often than those without (88% against 50%). No denominators or tests are given for these results.

No deaths were counted. The paper argues in both directions without measuring either: without uptake of the mandate, overdose deaths and the drugs involved may be undercounted (abstract, Discussion 5th paragraph), and coroners trained in toxicology use can reduce the listing of non-relevant drugs on certificates (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Policy Implication; Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the findings may not generalize to states with centralized medical-examiner systems; non-respondents may have answered differently; respondents may have presented themselves as complying with the law.

reporting_issues.issue: Years of service: Table 1's all-respondents column gives 20 (42.5%) under ten years and 27 (57.5%) ten or more, and the Results text follows it (43% and 58%); but the phase columns of the same rows sum to 27 and 20, and Tables 2 to 4 use n=27 for under ten years and n=20 for ten or more.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1, years serving rows; Results, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 to 4, column headings
reporting_issues.consequence: The stratified analyses use 27 under ten years and 20 with ten or more (editors' sums). Three placements agree on that split (the phase columns of Table 1, the column headings of Tables 3 and 4, and the row counts of Table 2), so the all-respondents column and the text are the likelier error; if they were right instead, every experience contrast in Tables 2 to 4 would be reversed. The text's 58% is 27 of 47 (57.4%) rounded twice.

reporting_issues.issue: Four p-values above 0.05 carry the asterisk defined as significant at the 0.05 level: limited finances by experience (0.0564), lack of staffing by region (0.0580) and the two Table 4 rows by region (0.0518 each). The text presents the finances and staffing contrasts as differences.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 and Table 4, p-value columns; Results, 4th and 6th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Those contrasts are not statistically supported; Fisher's exact tests give 0.105 and 0.086 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Time to collect samples by region: 7 of 22 Eastern-region coroners (31.8%) against 7 of 25 elsewhere (28%) is printed with p=0.0371 and described in the text as a significant difference; recomputed from those counts, chi-square p=0.78 and Fisher p=1.0 (editors' calculation). Discomfort with collection by training (8 of 39 against 1 of 7) is printed with p=0.3273; recomputed 0.70 and 1.0.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3, time involved and uncomfortable rows; Results, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: At least two printed p-values do not belong to their counts; the Eastern-region time barrier is not a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: Methods name chi-square and Fisher exact tests without saying which was used when. Recomputed from the printed counts (editors' calculation), the printed p-values match uncorrected chi-square in some rows, Fisher's exact test in others (0.0431, 0.0033, 0.0026) and, once, the likelihood-ratio chi-square (lack of facilities by experience, printed 0.0404; Pearson 0.046, Fisher 0.059). For time to collect by position (printed 0.0497) and information gained by experience (printed 0.0366), significance depends on the test: Fisher's exact test gives 0.062 and 0.064, and the continuity-corrected chi-square 0.10 and 0.075, although no expected count is below 5.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical Analysis; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Several subgroup differences described as significant, including the experience differences in valuing the information from testing and in lack of facilities, are fragile: they fall below 0.05 by uncorrected chi-square but not by Fisher's exact test.

reporting_issues.issue: Text against table: time involved in sample collection is a barrier for 19% in the Results text but 14 of 47 (30%) in Table 3; the Discussion's approximately one-half reporting increases in both toxicology testing and autopsy requests does not match Table 2 (58% and 35%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 6th paragraph; Table 3; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the table counts; the share reporting both increases is not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4 the row for presence of drug paraphernalia at the scene repeats every value of the toxicology-results row (18, 37.5%; 11 and 7; 14 and 4; 5 and 13; the same p-values).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 4, first two items
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a duplicated row; the true values for one of the two items are unknown, so neither should be cited by stratum beyond the text's 38% for toxicology results.

reporting_issues.issue: The text lists law enforcement (13%) among concurrent positions, with percentages summing above 100%; Table 1 has no law-enforcement row, and its four categories sum to exactly 48.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1, concurrent positions
reporting_issues.consequence: Concurrent positions should be cited from Table 1, as exclusive categories.

reporting_issues.issue: Printing errors in the tables: 'A,' in place of the 'yes' count for small jurisdictions in Table 2 (22, 59.5%, by subtraction); '(8122%)' and '(8282%)' in Table 3 for 22 (81.5%) and 22 (88%); Eastern 'information gained always helps' 13 (31.9%) where 13 of 22 is 59.1%, with 8 'not always' making 21; and percentages such as 40.1% for 11 of 27, 14.7% for 2 of 14, 63.3% for 7 of 11 and 55.6% for 12 of 22.
reporting_issues.consequence: Each cell must be recomputed from counts before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement of human rights says the article contains no studies on living human subjects and that ethical approval was not required, while the study is a survey of living coroners; no ethics review or consent procedure is described.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a threat to the data, but the ethics reporting is inconsistent with the design.

disagreements.first_pass: The title and first objective present the study as measuring the impact of the mandate, but impact was measured only through coroners' own reports. The Discussion opens by saying that approximately one-half of coroners reported increases in both toxicology testing and autopsy requests; Table 2 gives 58% for toxicology and 35% for autopsies, and the share reporting both is not given. The Conclusion states that the legislation "has had significant impacts" and that most Kentucky coroners reported more testing through increased autopsy referrals, which generalizes from 48 respondents to all coroners and is contradicted by the 35% who reported more autopsies. Experience differences in valuing testing and kits rest partly on uncorrected chi-square tests in small cells, and an Eastern-region difference of 32% against 28% is called statistically significant. The policy implication (without uptake, overdose deaths and the drugs involved may be undercounted) and the statement that trained coroners list fewer non-relevant drugs are arguments, not findings of this survey. The abstract's own conclusion, that uptake is not yet complete, is restrained.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 274 (agree, with an addition): the card calls the abstract's 'uptake not yet complete' restrained, but its basis is a non sequitur: coroners already testing before the mandate would also report no increase, and no item asked whether all decedents are tested (Discussion, 1st paragraph).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted (Discussion, 1st paragraph; no such item among those the Results report). 'Restrained' replaced by a description of the basis; the kits difference, which holds by Fisher's exact test (0.0094), taken out of the test-choice sentence.
